steps.body: Eleven is not a brand-new thing — it is ten and one more. The ten is finished; a single extra rides on top.
steps.narration: Eleven is not a brand-new thing — it is ten and one more. The ten is finished; a single extra rides on top.

widget.prompt: A full group of 10 is already shown. Add the extra dots needed to make 11.

commonCounts.feedback: 0 leaves 1 dots still missing — the ten alone only makes 10, not 11.
2 adds 1 too many; ten and 2 is 12, one past 11.

widget.missFeedback: The ten is done; count on from 10 while adding dots, and stop when you reach 11.
widget.successFeedback: 11 built — one complete ten and 1 more, exactly what the teen numeral says.

predict.prompt: A full ten, then one more dot. What number is that?
predict.reveal: The finished ten still counts; the new dot lifts the total one past it.

cml.actionGoal: Build one complete ten, then count on the ones, for knb ten plus one.
invariants: Every teen number is one complete ten and some ones — the left digit records the finished ten, the right digit counts the extras — and that split is what knb ten plus one rests on.
misconceptions: Reading the 1 of a teen as “one” instead of one TEN, or counting only the leftover ones and forgetting the completed ten.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one more dot joined the ones, which teen would the frame show then?

widget.prompt: Start at 10 and count on 1. Tap where you land.

commonLandings.feedback: 10 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 11.
12 goes one complete hop too far. Count just 1 hops from 10 to land on 11.

widget.missFeedback: Count 1 on from 10: you land on 11.
widget.successFeedback: 10 and 1 more is 11 — the teen numeral written as a walk: ten first, then the ones.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — all 1 counts past ten are needed to reach 11.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — the count-on stops after 1 numbers, on 11.

steps.narration: Say it as a walk: land on ten, take one more step. That step's name is eleven.

widget.prompt: A learner says 13 has three tens. Build only the three extra ones beside the finished ten to repair the model.

commonCounts.feedback: That shows one too few loose ones. The target needs 3.
That shows one too many loose ones. Stop at 3.

widget.missFeedback: Keep the full ten fixed and build exactly 3 loose ones.
widget.successFeedback: 13 is one complete ten and 3 more.

widget.prompt: What does the numeral 14 secretly say?

options.label: A one and a four, side by side
options.feedback: That reads the digits as neighbours; the left digit is a whole TEN, not a one.

options.label: One complete ten, and four more
options.feedback: Correct — the 1 stands for a whole ten, the 4 for the ones riding on top.

options.label: Four tens and a one
options.feedback: That swaps the digits' jobs — the ten is on the left, the ones on the right.

options.label: Fourteen separate tens
options.feedback: Only the single left digit counts tens; fourteen has exactly one of them.

widget.prompt: What number comes right after 16? Hop one and tap where you land.

commonLandings.feedback: 16 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 17.
18 goes one complete hop too far. One hop from 16 lands on 17.

widget.missFeedback: Count 1 on from 16: you land on 17.
widget.successFeedback: 17 — one hop forward; the teens follow the song exactly.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — a single hop forward reaches 17.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — right after 16 means one hop, stopping on 17.

widget.prompt: A group shows 12 dots. Which numeral names that amount?

options.feedback: That numeral names one more dot than the group shows.
That numeral stops one dot short; the ten plus the extras reaches 12.
Correct — a full ten and 2 more is what the numeral 12 says: 1 ten, 2 ones.
2 counts only the extras and forgets the whole completed ten underneath.
